prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Apollo 13 lifted off from Cape Kennedy on April 11, 1970, carrying three men toward what was meant to be the third landing on the Moon. The commander was Jim Lovell, who had already flown to lunar orbit on Apollo 8 and was making his fourth spaceflight. Fred Haise was the lunar module pilot and a first-time flier. The command module pilot was Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days earlier, after doctors grounded Ken Mattingly because he had been exposed to German measles. Swigert had trained as a backup and knew the spacecraft well, but he had barely practiced with Lovell and Haise as a team. The first two days were so uneventful that the crew and flight controllers alike began to regard the mission as routine, and the public, which had grown bored with moon shots, largely stopped watching.

That changed on the evening of April 13, about fifty-five hours into the flight and roughly two hundred thousand miles from home. Mission control asked Swigert to switch on the fans that stirred the supercold oxygen and hydrogen stored in the service module, a routine step meant to keep the contents from stratifying. Shortly afterward the crew heard a loud bang and felt the spacecraft shudder. Warning lights lit up, the voltage on the electrical buses dropped, and Swigert radioed the now famous understatement that they had a problem. Lovell repeated it for the controllers, and a few minutes later he looked out the window and saw gas streaming into space. Oxygen tank number two had ruptured, damaging the neighboring tank and blowing a panel off the side of the service module. The two tanks fed both the crew's air and the fuel cells that made the ship's electricity and drinking water, so within hours the command module was dying.

On the ground, flight director Gene Kranz and his team worked through the problem under enormous pressure. Controllers first suspected a faulty instrument, but the evidence soon made it clear that the ship was losing oxygen fast and would not have power for long. The landing was obviously off, and the question became whether the men could survive the trip home. The answer lay in the lunar module Aquarius, which was still attached and intact. It had been built to support two men for about two days on the Moon, but now it would serve as a lifeboat for three men for roughly four days. The crew shut down the command module, which they would need again for reentry, to preserve its small reserve of battery power, and Lovell and Haise climbed through into Aquarius while Swigert followed.

The next problem was geometry. Earlier in the flight the spacecraft had been moved off the trajectory that would loop it back to Earth without any engine burn, to prepare for the landing at Fra Mauro, and a simple turnaround was ruled out because the damaged service module engine could not be trusted. Instead, the planners chose to swing around the far side of the Moon and use the lunar module's descent engine to put the ship on a path home. The crew burned that engine shortly after passing the Moon, then burned it again about two hours after closest approach to shorten the trip by several hours. While looping behind the Moon they briefly became the farthest humans ever from Earth, at nearly two hundred and fifty thousand miles, a record that still stands. They had little time to appreciate it, because the spacecraft was cold, the batteries were limited, and every system had to be husbanded carefully.

Conditions inside Aquarius grew harsh. To save electricity the crew turned off nearly everything that was not essential, and the cabin temperature fell to a few degrees above freezing. Water condensed on the walls, and the men slept little in the bitter cold. Water was rationed to a few ounces per person each day, because it was needed to cool the electronics, and Haise developed a fever and a painful infection. Lovell and Swigert were also dehydrated and exhausted. A more urgent threat arose as the crew exhaled carbon dioxide, which built up in the cabin faster than the lunar module's small filters could remove it. The command module held spare filter canisters, but they were square and the lunar module's receptacles were round. Engineers on the ground assembled a makeshift adapter from items the crew had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a suit hose, and duct tape, and then read the instructions to the crew by radio. The improvised fitting worked, and the carbon dioxide level fell.

Navigation also became harder than anyone had planned. The usual guidance system was shut down to conserve power, and the lunar module's own system was never meant to steer the combined craft. The astronauts had to make a manual correction burn on the way home, using the Earth's terminator, the line between day and night, as a reference for pointing the spacecraft. Meanwhile, in the simulators on the ground, engineers, including Mattingly, worked out a procedure for restarting the command module with only the power left in its batteries, a sequence nobody had ever imagined needing. They wrote it out line by line and read it up to the crew, who would have to follow it in a cold, cramped cabin after days with almost no rest.

As the spacecraft approached Earth, the crew separated the damaged service module and, for the first time, saw how badly it had been hurt. A whole side panel was missing and the equipment inside was exposed and scorched, and Lovell reported it to Houston with obvious dismay. Nobody on the ground was sure whether the blast had also harmed the heat shield on the command module, and the crew could do nothing about it anyway. Last of all, they moved back into Odyssey, powered it up using the new procedure, and cast off Aquarius, which had saved their lives, to burn up in the atmosphere.

On April 17, the command module plunged into the atmosphere, and the usual communications blackout began. It lasted longer than expected, because the shallower path and slow speed stretched the ionized sheath around the capsule, and for several tense minutes there was only static. Then Swigert's voice came through, and soon after that three parachutes opened over the South Pacific. The capsule splashed down near Samoa within sight of the recovery ship Iwo Jima, a little under six days after launch. The men were weak and cold, and Haise was still ill, but all three were alive and soon recovered.

A review board later traced the accident to an earlier chain of small errors. The oxygen tank had been dropped slightly during handling before launch, and a damaged fill tube was never noticed. During a ground test, the heaters in the tank ran far longer than designed, and their thermostatic switches had been rated for a lower voltage than the one applied. This scorched the Teflon insulation on the wires inside, leaving bare conductors that sparked when Swigert turned on the stirring fans. Engineers redesigned the tanks and the wiring, and later Apollo missions flew without further trouble. Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, but it is remembered as a different kind of triumph, one in which careful improvisation by the crew and the ground team brought three men home from what looked like certain disaster.
